name: Checking AI Feedback Before Students See It
title: Checking AI Feedback Before Students See It
answer: Checking AI feedback before students see it means a teacher reads what a tool has said about an English learner's writing before that student reads it. It matters because language models can misread the ordinary features of multilingual writing, and AI detectors can wrongly flag non native speakers as cheaters. Reviewing first keeps confusing or unfair feedback from reaching the student.

sections.body: AI feedback on the writing of English learners can point a student in the wrong direction. When teachers examined a language model's comments, they found it misread variations that are common in the writing of multilingual learners. A feature that comes from a student's home language, or that simply shows English still developing, may be marked as a mistake, while a genuine error may pass unnoticed. A student handed feedback like that can lose confidence and still not learn what to fix. The idea here is that a teacher screens the tool's comments before the student reads them, so what arrives is feedback that treats a developing writer's language respectfully and helps them grow.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not sort this practice by grade band, so it applies wherever English learners are writing and a tool is commenting on their work. The teacher reviews the AI feedback before the student sees it, at least until the teacher has a sense of how a given tool handles that student's writing. A practical step is to pull a sample of the feedback, look for comments that misread the student's language, and adjust how the tool is set up in response. The aim is not to block feedback but to make sure what reaches the student is accurate and encouraging. Once a teacher knows how the tool behaves with a particular writer, the review can be shaped around what that tool and that student need.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports two research findings rather than giving a formal evidence label. Teachers who reviewed a language model's feedback found that it misread common variations in multilingual learners' writing (Barron et al., 2025). Separately, research has found that AI detectors frequently misclassify writing by non native English speakers as generated by AI (Liang et al., 2023). The text also notes that Chapter 6 recommended against relying on AI detection, and says that advice applies with special force to English learners.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by what the tools get wrong. Feedback can confuse or discourage a student, and a detector can accuse an English learner of cheating because of how they write, which the text calls a deep injustice. The decision about whether a piece of feedback is worth passing on stays with the teacher, who judges whether it treats a developing writer's language respectfully and helps them grow. The text's guidance is to review AI feedback before English learners see it, at least until a teacher knows how a tool handles their writing, and to adjust the tool's setup when the sample shows problems. Nothing in the text hands that judgment to the software.
